title: 4 · Skills & Custom Workflows
section: From one-off prompts to reusable procedures
text:
From one-off prompts to reusable procedures
By now you can direct an agent through a task. But researchers do the same kinds of tasks over and over: clean a new wave of a dataset the same way, build the same style of Table 1, format a manuscript to a journal’s requirements, run the same diagnostic checks on a model.
Retyping the instructions each time is exactly the repetition CLAUDE.md solved for project context. A skill solves it for procedures.









CLAUDE.md
Skill




Answers
“What should the agent always know about this project?”
“How do I do this recurring task, anywhere?”


When read
Every session, automatically
When the task comes up


Scope
One project
Reusable across projects


Example
“Data lives in data/; use tidyverse”
“Build a CONSORT-style participant-flow diagram”



A skill is, at its simplest, a named, packaged set of instructions for one recurring task — a description of when to use it and how to do it, written once and reused.

title: 4 · Skills & Custom Workflows
text:
Anatomy of a skill
A skill is a Markdown file with a bit of structured front matter. The two parts that matter most:
---
name: table-one
description: >
  Build a publication-ready "Table 1" (baseline characteristics by
  group) from a data frame. Use when the user asks for a descriptive
  or baseline characteristics table.
---

# Table One

## When to use
The user has a cleaned data frame and wants baseline characteristics
compared across a grouping variable (e.g., treatment arm).

## How to do it
1. Confirm the grouping variable and which covariates to include.
2. Use the `gtsummary` package (`tbl_summary()` + `add_p()` only if asked).
3. Continuous vars: median [IQR] unless clearly normal; categorical: n (%).
4. Label variables with human-readable names.
5. Output as a `gt` table saved to `tables/table1.html` and `.docx`.
6. Never fabricate values — read them from the data.

## Conventions
- Match the project's figure/table style in CLAUDE.md.
- Show me the code and the rendered table before saving.






TipThe description is the most important line



The agent decides whether to use a skill by reading its description. Make it specific about when the skill applies and what it produces. Vague descriptions (“helps with tables”) get ignored or misfired; concrete ones (“build a baseline-characteristics Table 1 from a data frame”) get invoked at the right moment.

title: 4 · Skills & Custom Workflows
section: What makes a good research skill
text:
What makes a good research skill

One clear job. A skill that does one thing well beats a kitchen-sink skill. “Format to JAMA figure specs” not “do all my figures.”
Encodes your standards. The whole point is that it captures how you like it done — your palette, your table style, your statistical conventions — so you stop re-explaining.
Has a done-condition. Say what the finished output looks like and where it goes.
Includes guardrails. “Read values from the data, never fabricate.” “Show me before saving.” Judgment stays with you.
Is reviewable. Because it’s a plain Markdown file in your repo, you can version it, diff it, and share it — a skill is itself reproducible documentation of a procedure.

title: 4 · Skills & Custom Workflows
text:
Where skills live
In Claude Code, skills live in a skills/ (or .claude/skills/) folder — project-level (shared via the repo) or personal (across all your projects). Because they’re just files in git, sharing a skill with a collaborator is a git push; adopting theirs is a git pull. Your lab’s conventions become executable.






NoteSkill vs. “workflow”



People use workflow loosely for a repeatable multi-step process. In practice you’ll build workflows by combining: a CLAUDE.md (project context) + one or more skills (procedures) + the git branch→PR→merge loop (control). Today’s build session is where you start assembling yours.








NotePortability beyond Claude Code



The SKILL.md format is Claude Code’s, but the asset is tool-agnostic: a well-written procedure in plain Markdown. Codex and other tools have their own mechanisms for reusable instructions (custom prompts, AGENTS.md sections), and the same file usually ports with minutes of rearranging. The hard part — articulating how you want the task done — is the part you’re writing today, and it survives every tool change.

title: 4 · Skills & Custom Workflows
text:
Good candidates from health-decision research
Skills worth writing (steal these for Exercise 4):

Table 1 builder — baseline characteristics to your house style.
Journal-figure formatter — apply JAMA/NEJM/Annals figure specs to a ggplot.
Reproducible-pipeline scaffold — set up data/, R/, numbered scripts, a 00_run_all.R, and a README, the way you always structure a project.
Reviewer-response drafter — turn reviewer comments + your notes into a structured point-by-point response.
Model diagnostics — run your standard set of checks (convergence, balance, sensitivity) on a fitted model and summarize.
Simulation calibration report — compare simulated outputs to targets and flag mismatches.







WarningSkills don’t remove your judgment



A skill makes a procedure repeatable — it does not make the decision correct. A “run my causal analysis” skill will faithfully run the wrong estimand if you point it at the wrong question. Bake verification and “show me before you commit” into every skill.



What to remember

A skill = a named, reusable procedure for a recurring task; the description decides when it fires.
Good skills do one job, encode your standards, state a done-condition, and include guardrails.
Skills are plain files in git — versioned, diffable, shareable with your lab.
Assemble workflows from CLAUDE.md + skills + the git review loop.

text:
Glossary







Term
Meaning




Agent
An LLM that can use tools (read/write files, run code, search) in a loop to complete tasks.


Agentic loop
Act → observe result → decide next action → repeat, until done or it needs you.


Branch
A parallel line of work in git; a sandbox that doesn’t touch main.


CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md
A project (or global) file of standing instructions an agent reads each session. AGENTS.md is the cross-tool convention (Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, …); CLAUDE.md is Claude Code’s name for it.


Commit
A saved snapshot of your files in git, with a message.


Context window
How much text (files, instructions, conversation) the model can “see” at once.


Diff
The line-by-line difference between two versions — your review surface.


gh
The GitHub command-line tool, used for auth and pull requests.


Hallucination
A plausible-but-false statement from a model; the reason we verify.


LLM
Large language model — the model underneath the agent.


MCP
Model Context Protocol — a standard for giving agents extra tools/data sources.


Merge
Combining an approved branch into main; your explicit “keep this.”


Prompt
What you ask the agent (and the skill of asking well).


Pull request (PR)
A proposal on GitHub to merge a branch, with a reviewable diff.


Repository (repo)
A folder tracked by git.


Skill
A reusable, packaged procedure for a recurring task.


Token
The unit LLMs read/write text in (~¾ of a word); measures context and cost.


Workflow
A repeatable multi-step process, assembled from CLAUDE.md + skills + the git loop.

title: 3 · Git & GitHub
section: Why git first, before turning an agent loose
text:
Why git first, before turning an agent loose
An agent is fast and will happily rewrite twelve files in thirty seconds. Without version control, that’s terrifying: you can’t tell what changed, can’t undo cleanly, and can’t separate its work from yours.
With git, the same speed is safe. Reframe the tools:







Git concept
Reframed for agent work




Commit
A save point you can always return to. Undo is free.


Branch
A sandbox where the agent can experiment without touching your working code.


Diff
The exact, line-by-line record of what the agent changed — your review surface.


Pull request (PR)
The gate: nothing reaches your main code until you approve the diff.


Merge
Your explicit “yes, keep this” decision.









ImportantThe core loop of this whole course



agent works on a branch → you review the diff in a pull request → you merge only what you approve.
Everything else is detail. This loop is what lets you move fast and stay in control.

title: 3 · Git & GitHub
text:
Git in ten minutes
A repository (“repo”) is a folder git is tracking. Work flows through three places: your files → the staging area (what you’re about to save) → a commit (a saved snapshot).
git init                      # start tracking this folder
git status                    # what's changed / staged?
git add R/01_clean.R          # stage a file for the next commit
git add .                     # stage everything changed
git commit -m "Clean cohort"  # save a snapshot with a message
git log --oneline             # history of commits
Commit messages are notes to your future self (and reviewers). Write them in the imperative: “Add cost-effectiveness model”, “Fix join dropping rows”. Small, frequent commits beat rare giant ones — they make history readable and undo precise.






TipYou can have the agent do the git for you



You don’t have to type these. In Claude Code you can say “commit this with a sensible message” or “make a branch called clean-data and work there.” You still decide when to commit and merge — the agent just does the mechanics. Learn the commands anyway, so you understand what it’s doing.

title: 3 · Git & GitHub
text:
Branches: the agent’s sandbox
A branch is a parallel line of work. main stays stable; the agent plays on a branch.
git switch -c feature/clean-data   # create + move to a new branch
# ... agent makes changes, you commit them ...
git switch main                    # your safe, untouched main
git switch feature/clean-data      # back to the work
If the branch goes sideways, you throw it away — main never saw it. This is the single most important habit for working with agents: let them work on a branch, not on main.

title: 3 · Git & GitHub
section: GitHub & pull requests: the review gate
text:
GitHub & pull requests: the review gate
GitHub is where repos live online — for backup, collaboration, and (crucially) pull requests. A PR says: “here’s a branch; here’s the diff; should we merge it into main?” It’s a purpose-built review surface with line-by-line comments.
Using the gh CLI (installed in Setup):
# push your branch to GitHub
git push -u origin feature/clean-data

# open a pull request from that branch into main
gh pr create --title "Clean cohort data" --body "Adds R/01_clean.R; drops missing age; recodes sex."

# review the change — read the diff!
gh pr diff

# when you're satisfied, merge and tidy up
gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch
The gh pr diff step is the one that matters. Read it. This is where you catch the dropped rows, the renamed column, the thing you didn’t ask for. Merging is you saying “I’ve reviewed this and I approve.”






WarningDestructive commands — gate these



Some git operations are hard or impossible to undo. Don’t let an agent run them unprompted, and be sure you understand them yourself:

git reset --hard — discards uncommitted work permanently.
git push --force — can overwrite others’ history on a shared branch.
git clean -fd — deletes untracked files from disk.

A good rule for your CLAUDE.md: “Never run destructive git commands (reset –hard, force push, clean) without asking.”

title: 3 · Git & GitHub
section: A complete session, start to finish
text:
A complete session, start to finish
Here’s the whole loop in one place — the pattern for every agent-assisted change:
# 1. start clean, on main
git switch main && git pull

# 2. branch for the task
git switch -c feature/cost-model

# 3. direct the agent to do the work (in Claude Code), review each step,
#    and commit in small pieces:
#    "Add the Markov cost model in R/02_model.R. Show me the diff, then commit."

# 4. push and open a PR
git push -u origin feature/cost-model
gh pr create --fill

# 5. REVIEW the diff — the gate
gh pr diff

# 6. approve by merging; delete the branch
gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch

# 7. back to a clean main with your approved change
git switch main && git pull






NoteSolo researcher? You still want this.



PRs aren’t just for teams. Even working alone, the branch-and-PR loop gives you a forced review step and a clean, documented history — exactly the reproducibility and control you want when an agent is writing the code.

title: 3 · Git & GitHub
text:
Beyond the loop: verification infrastructure
The branch → PR → merge loop is the floor. Researchers who run whole projects this way add a few habits that turn a git repo into verification infrastructure — a system where every number can be traced and every decision is on the record. (These come from Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham’s agentic research workflow; they port beautifully to health decision science.)
1 · Ask for verifiability in the prompt, before the work happens. Don’t inspect for auditability after the fact — make it part of the spec:
Implement the cost model in R/02_model.R. Requirements: every number in
the results table must be produced by code (no hand-typed values); write
the sample-attrition counts at each exclusion step to tables/attrition.csv;
and log any modeling decision you make in LOG.md with one line of rationale.
2 · Keep DECISIONS.md and LOG.md in the repo. Two plain-text files, committed like everything else:

DECISIONS.md — the why behind consequential choices (“used gamma frailty over lognormal because…”), written when the decision is made. Your future methods section and reviewer responses, pre-drafted.
LOG.md — a running lab notebook of what was done, by you or the agent. Cheap to write, priceless at revision time.

3 · Use GitHub issues as the feedback loop. Instead of holding tasks in your head (or a wandering chat session), file them as issues — “validate the model against published Table 3”, “cost totals look 10% high, investigate.” Then point a fresh agent session at an issue: it reads the issue, orients in the repo, fixes, and the PR closes it. Issues give you a to-do list, a paper trail, and a clean way for coauthors (human or agent) to pick up work.
4 · Every number flows from code. No copy-pasting results into the manuscript. Figures and tables are emitted as files by scripts; the document pulls them in. When a reviewer asks “where did this hazard ratio come from,” the answer is a five-minute provenance trace: number → table file → script → commit → the logged rationale in DECISIONS.md.






TipTry it on the demo repo



A good live test of all four at once: “File an issue to restructure analysis.R into a pipeline. Then, in a fresh session, read the issue, do the work on a branch with every output written by code, log decisions in DECISIONS.md, and open a PR that closes the issue.”



What to remember

Commit = save point · branch = sandbox · PR = review gate · merge = your “yes.”
The core loop: agent works on a branch → you review the diff → you merge what you approve.
Keep the agent off main. Read the diff before every merge.
Gate destructive commands (reset --hard, force push, clean) — put it in CLAUDE.md.
Level up: ask for verifiability in the prompt, keep DECISIONS.md/LOG.md, drive work through issues, and make every number flow from code.

title: 1 · Foundations of Agentic Coding
text: Module goal: Leave with a durable mental model — four mechanisms that explain what agents are, why they work where they work, and what they change about doing research. Tools will age out; these won’t. · Slides

title: 1 · Foundations of Agentic Coding
section: The shift: from writing to directing
text:
The shift: from writing to directing
For decades, programming meant typing every line yourself. Agentic coding changes the unit of work. You describe what you want; the agent reads your files, writes code, runs it, reads the errors, and fixes them — then you review and decide what to keep.
You move from author to director. Your value shifts from remembering syntax to specifying intent clearly, reviewing critically, and keeping control. That last part is what the rest of this course is really about.

title: 1 · Foundations of Agentic Coding
text:
Mechanisms, not tools
This course teaches with Claude Code, but Claude Code is just the current instance. OpenAI’s Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, and whatever ships next year all work the same way underneath. The specific tools and their config syntax will age quickly; the mechanisms below won’t. Learn the mechanisms, and every new tool is a five-minute adjustment.






This framing — and much of this module — is adapted from Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham’s excellent NBER SI 2026 materials on agentic AI for research, reworked for health decision science.



The landscape, so you can place whatever you encounter:








Category
What it is
Examples (mid-2026)




Terminal / CLI agents
An agent in your terminal, working on your files and repos directly
Claude Code (this course), OpenAI Codex CLI, Gemini CLI


IDE-integrated
Agents inside your editor
VS Code extensions (Claude Code, Codex), Cursor, JetBrains


Chat + code
Chat assistants that write code but don’t run in your project
claude.ai, ChatGPT, Gemini


Cloud / async agents
Agents that run on a server, e.g., picking up a GitHub issue or PR
Codex (cloud), Claude Code (web), GitHub coding agents



Every one of these — and whatever replaces them — runs on the same four mechanisms:








#
Mechanism
One-line claim




M1
The agent loop
LLM + tools + feedback ≠ chatbot: it acts, observes, iterates


M2
Context is the scarce resource
The durable skill is engineering what the model sees


M3
You are the principal
This is delegation: specify, decompose, monitor, verify


M4
Verification asymmetry
Agents excel exactly where checking their work is cheap

title: 1 · Foundations of Agentic Coding
text:
M1 · The agent loop
Strip away the hype and an agent is three things:

A large language model (LLM) — a model that predicts text, and is very good at turning descriptions into code.
Tools — the model can call functions: read a file, write a file, run a shell command, search, run your tests.
A loop — the model takes an action, observes the result, and decides the next action, repeating until the task is done or it needs you.

        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │                                           │
   you ─┴─► LLM ──► pick a tool ──► run it ──► read the result
             ▲                                     │
             └──────────── decide next ◄───────────┘
                        (repeat until done)
A chatbot answers; an agent acts, checks its work, and iterates in your actual project. This is why an agent can debug a simulation that won’t converge or fix a data-join that drops rows without you round-tripping every message: it runs your code, reads the error, and tries again.






TipDemo (do this live)



Point back at the task dictated at 8:35 — it’s been looping while we talked: acting, hitting errors, reading them, fixing. We’ll review its work shortly — reviewing, not admiring.

title: 1 · Foundations of Agentic Coding
section: M2 · Context is the scarce resource
text:
M2 · Context is the scarce resource
The model can only reason about what’s in its context window — the files, instructions, and conversation it currently “sees.” Almost every frustrating agent session traces back to context: too little (it guesses and invents column names) or too much and stale (it loses the thread).
The durable skill is staging context deliberately: pointing the agent at the right files, providing the data dictionary, the relevant paper, the error message — and writing standing context down once (CLAUDE.md, Module 2) instead of re-explaining every session. Tools differ in config syntax; this skill transfers to all of them.

title: 1 · Foundations of Agentic Coding
text:
M3 · You are the principal
Working with an agent is a delegation problem — the same one you face with a research assistant. The economics are familiar:

Specify the task and the done-condition (Module 2)
Decompose big asks into small, checkable steps
Monitor while it works (watch the diffs, not the vibes)
Verify before you accept (Module 3 makes this structural)

The skills that appreciate in value as agents get better: taste (what’s worth doing), specification (saying precisely what you want), and skepticism (knowing when to distrust the output). The skill that depreciates: typing speed.

title: 1 · Foundations of Agentic Coding
text:
M4 · Verification asymmetry
The most useful predictive rule in this course: agents excel exactly where checking their work is cheap.
Code is unusually verifiable — it runs or it doesn’t, tests pass or fail, the figure renders or it doesn’t, row counts match or they don’t. That’s why coding is the breakout agent application. And it predicts, task by task, where agents will help your research:

Cheap to verify → strong fitsExpensive to verify → handle with care



Boilerplate & glue: reshaping data, join pipelines — check the row counts.
Debugging: the error either goes away or it doesn’t.
Refactoring: same outputs before and after — diffable, testable.
Simulation scaffolding: structure you then inspect and parameterize.
Figures & tables: you can see whether it’s right.
Documentation & READMEs: quick to read and correct.




Statistical / causal judgment: the agent will happily run a model that’s wrong for your question. The estimand is yours to own — checking it requires exactly the expertise you were hoping to save.
Domain facts: a plausible-but-wrong parameter, transition probability, or citation looks identical to a right one. Verify against sources.
Anything irreversible: deleting files, force-pushing, touching real data — gate these (Module 3).
Confidential data: know your IRB/data-use rules before pointing any agent at PHI.










WarningThe one rule that makes all of this safe



Never merge what you haven’t reviewed. Agents are fast and confident, and sometimes confidently wrong. The productivity gain is real only if you keep a review step — which is exactly why we spend a whole module on git.

title: 1 · Foundations of Agentic Coding
section: The catch: the pain points move
text:
The catch: the pain points move
Honesty for researchers: agentic coding makes execution dramatically cheaper — but that doesn’t make research easier overall. The pain moves:

Verification debt. Production cost collapsed; verification cost didn’t. Understanding what your agent did is itself costly time — and if you skip it, you’re accumulating debt that comes due at revision, replication, or retraction time.
Judgment is still king. Study design, estimand choice, model structure, what sensitivity analyses matter — none of it got easier, and agents actively gravitate toward the well-trodden default over the right choice for your question.
Ideas at a premium. When execution is cheap, the bar rises for how far you push the analysis — and for having questions worth asking in the first place.
Data access doesn’t budge. An agent can’t get you a claims-data DUA or IRB approval.

The researchers who benefit most aren’t the ones who delegate everything — they’re the ones who redeploy the saved execution time into verification, design, and ideas.

title: 1 · Foundations of Agentic Coding
text:
Reproducibility: an underrated win
Because an agent works in a repo, everything it does is inspectable and versioned. Done well, agentic coding pushes you toward better reproducibility than typing everything yourself: scripted pipelines, committed history, and prose (in CLAUDE.md and skills) that documents how the project is meant to be run — the kind of thing you can drop straight into a methods supplement.

title: 1 · Foundations of Agentic Coding
text:
Vocabulary you’ll hear today
Keep this handy; full glossary in Resources.







Term
Plain-English meaning




LLM
The underlying model (e.g., Claude, GPT) that turns your words into code and decisions.


Token
The unit an LLM reads/writes text in (~¾ of a word). “Context” and cost are measured in tokens.


Context window
How much text the model can “see” at once — your files, instructions, and the conversation so far.


Prompt
What you ask for. Also the skill of asking well.


Tool / tool call
An action the agent can take (read, edit, run, search).


Agentic loop
Act → observe → decide → repeat (M1).


CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md
A project file of standing instructions the agent reads every session (Module 2). AGENTS.md is the cross-tool convention; CLAUDE.md is Claude Code’s.


Skill
A reusable, packaged instruction set for a recurring task (Module 4).


Hallucination
When a model states something plausible but false — the reason we review.


MCP
“Model Context Protocol” — a standard way to give agents extra tools/data sources.




What to remember

M1: an agent = LLM + tools + a loop — it acts, checks, and iterates in your real project.
M2: context is the scarce resource; staging it well is the durable skill.
M3: you’re the principal — specify, decompose, monitor, verify. Taste and skepticism appreciate.
M4: agents excel where verification is cheap — that predicts, task by task, where they’ll help you.
Execution got cheaper; verification, judgment, and ideas didn’t. Spend the savings there.

title: Exercise 4 · Write Your First Skill
text: Time: ~12 min · Pairs with: Skills & Workflows · Goal: a working, reusable skill that captures how you like a recurring task done. This is the thing you take home.

title: Exercise 4 · Write Your First Skill
section: 1 · Pick a task you repeat (2 min)
text:
1 · Pick a task you repeat (2 min)
Choose one recurring task where you keep re-explaining your preferences. Steal one of these if nothing jumps out:

Table 1 builder — baseline characteristics to your house style.
Figure formatter — apply your (or a journal’s) figure specs to a plot.
Project scaffold — set up a reproducible repo the way you always do.
Reviewer-response drafter — comments + notes → point-by-point response.
Model diagnostics — run your standard checks on a fitted model.

title: Exercise 4 · Write Your First Skill
section: 2 · Draft it from the template (5 min)

title: Exercise 4 · Write Your First Skill
section: 3 · Install it where Claude Code will find it (2 min)
text:
3 · Install it where Claude Code will find it (2 min)
Save the file into your skills folder (project-level so it travels with the repo):
mkdir -p .claude/skills/table-one
# save your file as .claude/skills/table-one/SKILL.md
(Adjust the name to your skill.) Commit it:
git add .claude/skills
git commit -m "Add table-one skill"

title: Exercise 4 · Write Your First Skill
section: 4 · Test it on real input (3 min)
text:
4 · Test it on real input (3 min)
Start a fresh session and trigger the skill with a natural request — don’t name the skill explicitly; see if the description makes it fire:
I have a cleaned data frame with age, sex, and treatment arm. Build me a
baseline characteristics table.
Watch whether the agent applies your conventions from the skill. If it doesn’t fire, your description probably isn’t specific enough about when to use it — tighten it and retry.

title: Exercise 4 · Write Your First Skill
text:
You’re done when…

You have a SKILL.md with a specific description and clear steps.
It includes at least one guardrail (“show me before saving” / “never fabricate”).
It’s saved in your skills folder and committed.
A natural-language request triggered the skill and produced output in your style.







NoteShare it



A skill is just a file in git. git push, send a labmate the repo, and they git pull — now your lab shares an executable convention. This is how a workflow spreads.


Next: Exercise 5 · Your own workflow →

title: Exercise 2 · Git with an Agent
text:
Time: ~15 min · Pairs with: Git & GitHub · Goal: run the core control loop end-to-end, so you trust an agent with real code.
We’ll continue in the agentic-ex1 folder from Exercise 1 (or make a fresh one). By the end you’ll have a change reviewed and merged through a real pull request.

title: Exercise 2 · Git with an Agent
section: 1 · Make it a repo and put it on GitHub (3 min)
text:
1 · Make it a repo and put it on GitHub (3 min)
cd agentic-ex1          # or your Exercise 1 folder
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial synthetic-data scripts"
gh repo create agentic-ex1 --private --source=. --push
gh repo create makes the GitHub repo and pushes main in one step. (Use --private for a throwaway.)

title: Exercise 2 · Git with an Agent
text:
2 · Branch for the change (1 min)
Never work on main. Ask the agent — or type it yourself:
git switch -c feature/add-summary-table
Or say to Claude Code: “Create a branch called feature/add-summary-table and work there.”

title: Exercise 2 · Git with an Agent
section: 3 · Direct the change, in small commits (5 min)
text:
3 · Direct the change, in small commits (5 min)
Give the agent a real task and have it commit as it goes:
On this branch: add a script `table.R` that writes a summary table of
mean and SD of cost by treatment arm to tables/summary.csv. Show me the
diff, then commit it with a clear message.
Review what it shows you. Then:
Also add a one-line note about this table to the README, and commit that
separately.
Check your history:
git log --oneline
You should see two small, clearly-labelled commits.

title: Exercise 2 · Git with an Agent
text:
4 · Open a pull request (2 min)
git push -u origin feature/add-summary-table
gh pr create --title "Add cost summary table" --fill
Or let the agent do it: “Push this branch and open a pull request into main.”

title: Exercise 2 · Git with an Agent
section: 5 · Review the diff — the gate (2 min)
text:
5 · Review the diff — the gate (2 min)
This is the whole point. Read the change before you accept it:
gh pr diff
Ask yourself: is this only what I asked for? Any surprise edits? Right files?






TipPractice catching something



Before merging, ask the agent to “add a totals row to the summary table.” Re-run gh pr diff and find that new change in the diff. Seeing your review surface update is the muscle you’re building.

title: Exercise 2 · Git with an Agent
text:
6 · Merge what you approve (1 min)
gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch
git switch main && git pull
Your approved change is now on main; the branch is cleaned up; main never saw the messy middle.

title: Exercise 2 · Git with an Agent
text:
You’re done when…

Your repo is on GitHub with main pushed.
You made a change on a branch, in at least two small commits.
You opened a pull request and ran gh pr diff to review it.
You merged it and returned to a clean main.







WarningIf something breaks




gh: not authenticated → run gh auth login (see Setup).
Pushed to the wrong branch? You’re on a throwaway repo — safe to experiment. Try git switch main and start the branch again.
Don’t run git push --force or git reset --hard to “fix” things right now — ask a facilitator first.

title: Agenda
text:
What to have open

This website.
A terminal in a folder where you can make a scratch project.
Claude Code (claude), signed in.
Your GitHub account in a browser tab.
A research task in mind for the build session.

title: 5 · Build Session
text: Module goal: Put it all together on your work. Leave with a repo, a CLAUDE.md, at least one skill, and a change you shipped through the branch→PR→merge loop. This module is Exercise 5 — facilitators circulate to help.

title: 5 · Build Session
text:
The idea
The rest of the course is hands-on. You’ll take one real task from your research and start building an agentic workflow around it — combining everything from the morning:

Foundations → you know what the agent is doing.
Prompting → you specify tasks well and review critically.
Git & GitHub → you keep the agent on a branch and merge only what you approve.
Skills → you package the repeatable part so it pays off again next week.

You won’t finish a whole project in 35 minutes — that’s not the goal. The goal is a working prototype and momentum: a repo set up correctly, one skill written, one change shipped, and a clear next step.

title: 5 · Build Session
text:
Pick a task (2 min)
Choose something small enough to make real progress on but real enough to matter. Good candidates:

A data-cleaning step for a dataset you’re working with now.
A figure you keep remaking — turn it into a formatter skill.
A simulation or model scaffold (Markov / microsimulation structure) you can flesh out later.
A manuscript task: methods section, reviewer response, README for a repo.
A project scaffold: set up a new analysis repo the way you always wish you had.







TipIf you’re stuck choosing



Pick the task you most dread repeating. That’s the one where a workflow pays off fastest — and dread is a great filter for “worth automating.”

title: 5 · Build Session
text:
Suggested path (≈30 min)
Work through as many as you can; each stands alone.

1 · Set up the repo (5 min)
mkdir my-workflow && cd my-workflow
git init
claude
Then ask the agent to scaffold a reproducible structure: > “Set up a reproducible R (or Python) project: data/raw, data/clean, R/ (or src/), figs/, a .gitignore, and a README. Make the first commit.”


2 · Write a CLAUDE.md (5 min)
Use the template and Exercise 3. Capture what the project does, its structure, how to run it, your conventions, and your guardrails. Commit it.


3 · Ship one change through a PR (10 min)
Direct the agent to do your actual task on a branch, review the diff, and merge it — the loop from Module 3:
git switch -c feature/first-task
# ... direct the agent; review; commit ...
git push -u origin feature/first-task   # (after gh repo create if needed)
gh pr create --fill
gh pr diff        # review!
gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch


4 · Write a skill (10 min)
Find the part of your task you’ll repeat and package it as a skill (Exercise 4, template). Commit it into the repo so it travels with the project.

title: 5 · Build Session
text:
Checkpoints — where you should be



Time
You should have…




+5 min
A git repo with a scaffolded structure and a first commit


+10 min
A CLAUDE.md describing the project and your guardrails


+20 min
One change shipped through a branch → PR → merge


+30 min
One skill written and committed

title: 5 · Build Session
text:
“Done” for today
You’re done when you can answer yes to all of these:

I have a repo (local, ideally pushed to GitHub) for a real task.
It has a CLAUDE.md an agent reads at the start of each session.
I directed an agent through at least one branch → PR → review → merge.
I wrote at least one skill that captures something I’ll do again.
I know my next step to keep developing this after today.







NoteGetting help



Drop questions in the Zoom chat and facilitators will jump into breakout rooms. Stuck on git? Show your git status and gh pr diff. Stuck on the agent? Share the prompt you used — usually the fix is a more specific prompt.

title: 5 · Build Session
text:
Where to go next

Grow your CLAUDE.md and skills as you notice yourself re-explaining things.
Share a skill with a labmate (git push) — build a shared team library.
Bring the branch→PR→merge loop to your existing repos, not just new ones.
Revisit the Resources page for cheat sheets and deeper reading.


What to remember

A workflow = project scaffold + CLAUDE.md + skills + the git review loop, assembled around a real task.
Aim for a working prototype and momentum, not a finished project.
Automate the task you most dread repeating — that’s where it pays off first.


Wrap-up: share what you built, and see Resources to keep going.

title: Exercise 1 · Your First Agent Session
text: Time: ~10 min · Pairs with: Prompting & Directing · Goal: feel the specify → act → review loop on a small, real task.

title: Exercise 1 · Your First Agent Session
text:
Setup (1 min)
Make a fresh scratch folder and start the agent:
mkdir agentic-ex1 && cd agentic-ex1
claude

title: Exercise 1 · Your First Agent Session
section: Task (do it twice — vague, then specified)
text:
Task (do it twice — vague, then specified)
We’ll generate a tiny synthetic dataset and a summary, so everyone has something concrete to review.

Round 1 — a vague prompt
Type this to the agent, exactly as-is:
make me some fake patient data and summarize it
Watch what it does. It will work — but notice all the choices it made for you (columns, size, format, what “summarize” means).


Round 2 — a specified prompt
Now ask for what you actually want:
Create an R script `make_data.R` that generates a synthetic dataset of
200 patients with columns: id, age (18–90), sex (M/F), treatment
(control/drug), and cost (positive, right-skewed). Save it to
data/patients.csv. Then create `summarize.R` that prints mean cost by
treatment arm and saves a colorblind-safe bar chart of it to
figs/cost_by_arm.png. Show me each script before running it.

title: Exercise 1 · Your First Agent Session
text:
Practice the loop

When it proposes a script, read it before you let it run. Does it do what you asked?
Ask it to run the scripts and show you the output and the figure path.
Give one piece of specific feedback, e.g.:
Make the cost distribution more skewed (use rgamma), and add
value labels on the bars.
Notice how a precise correction lands in one turn.







TipTry a plan-first prompt



Before round 2, you can add: “Before writing anything, tell me your plan and which files you’ll create.” Approve it, then let it go. This is the habit we formalize with git next.

title: Exercise 1 · Your First Agent Session
text:
You’re done when…

You ran both the vague and the specified prompt and can articulate the difference in results.
data/patients.csv and figs/cost_by_arm.png exist and look right.
You gave at least one specific correction and the agent applied it.
You read at least one script before it ran.

title: Exercise 1 · Your First Agent Session
text:
Reflect (30 sec)
What did the vague prompt get wrong that the specified one fixed? That gap is the value you add as the director.

title: Exercise 3 · Write a CLAUDE.md
text:
Time: ~10 min · Pairs with: Git & GitHub and Prompting · Goal: a CLAUDE.md that makes the agent behave like it already knows your project.
Now move onto a project that matters to you (or keep using agentic-ex1). You’ll write the file Claude Code reads at the start of every session.

title: Exercise 3 · Write a CLAUDE.md
text:
1 · Start from the template (2 min)
Open the annotated CLAUDE.md template and copy it into your project root as CLAUDE.md. Or have the agent do the first draft:
Read the files in this repo, then draft a CLAUDE.md that describes what
this project does, its folder structure, how to run it, my coding
conventions, and guardrails. Ask me anything you can't infer.
Letting the agent draft it from your actual repo is often the fastest start — then you correct it.

title: Exercise 3 · Write a CLAUDE.md
section: 2 · Make sure it covers the five things (5 min)
text:
2 · Make sure it covers the five things (5 min)
A useful research CLAUDE.md answers:

What this repo does — one paragraph: the question and what the code produces.
Structure — what lives where (data/raw, R/, figs/, …).
How to run it — the one command or script that reproduces everything.
Conventions — language, style, figure preferences, naming.
Guardrails — what the agent must not do without asking.







TipGuardrails are the highest-value lines



The instructions that save you grief:
## Guardrails
- Never modify anything in data/raw/.
- Never run destructive git commands (reset --hard, force push, clean) without asking.
- Don't install packages without asking.
- Make changes on a branch; show me the diff before committing.

title: Exercise 3 · Write a CLAUDE.md
text:
3 · Test that it works (2 min)
Commit the file, then start a fresh session and give a task that relies on the context:
Where does cleaned data get written, and how do I reproduce the whole
pipeline?
If the agent answers correctly without you explaining, your CLAUDE.md is doing its job. Commit it:
git add CLAUDE.md
git commit -m "Add CLAUDE.md with project context and guardrails"

title: Exercise 3 · Write a CLAUDE.md
text:
4 · (Bonus) your global CLAUDE.md

title: 2 · Prompting & Directing Agents
text:
Prompting is specification, not incantation
There are no magic words. A good prompt is just a clear specification of intent, context, and constraints. The mental shift: talk to the agent the way you’d brief a capable new research assistant who is fast, literal, and doesn’t know your project yet.
Four ingredients turn a vague ask into a good one:








Ingredient
Weak
Strong




Goal
“clean the data”
“drop rows with missing age, and recode sex to a factor with labels Male/Female”


Context
(none)
“the raw file is data/raw/cohort.csv; the cleaning script is R/01_clean.R”


Constraints
(none)
“use tidyverse, keep it readable, don’t change the column names downstream code expects”


Done-condition
(none)
“it works when 01_clean.R runs without warnings and writes data/clean/cohort.rds”

title: 2 · Prompting & Directing Agents
section: Six habits that make agents work
text:
Six habits that make agents work

State the goal and the done-condition. “How do you know it’s finished?” is the single most useful sentence to add.
Point at the context. Name the files, the function, the error. Agents are great at reading your repo — tell them where to look instead of describing from memory.
Plan before acting on anything non-trivial. Ask for a plan first: “Before editing, tell me your approach and which files you’ll change.” Then approve or redirect. Cheap to steer early, expensive to unwind later.
Work in small steps. One change, review, next. Matches Jacob’s “small testable steps over big rewrites” default and keeps diffs reviewable.
Make it show its work. “Run the tests.” “Show me the diff.” “Print the first 5 rows.” You’re verifying, not trusting.
Correct with specifics. Not “that’s wrong” but “the join dropped 12 rows — use a left join keyed on id.” Precise feedback closes the loop fast.







TipDemo (do this live)



Take a deliberately vague prompt (“make a figure of the results”) and a specified one (“plot mean cost by treatment arm as a grouped bar chart with 95% CIs, colorblind-safe palette, save to figs/cost_by_arm.png at 300 dpi”) — run both and compare. The difference sells the whole module.

title: 2 · Prompting & Directing Agents
text:
Scope the context deliberately
The agent can only reason about what’s in its context window. Two failure modes:

Too little: it guesses about files it hasn’t seen and invents column names. → Point it at the files.
Too much / stale: a long, wandering session accumulates dead ends and the agent loses the thread. → Start a fresh session for a new task. A clean context is often the fix for a confused agent.

Rule of thumb: one session, one coherent task. When you switch to something unrelated, start over.

title: 2 · Prompting & Directing Agents
text:
Plan-then-act, concretely
For anything beyond a one-liner, split the work in two:
Before you change any files: read R/01_clean.R and data/raw/cohort.csv,
then tell me your plan for the cleaning step and exactly which files
you'll create or modify. Wait for my OK.
Review the plan. Then:
Looks good — go ahead. Make the changes on a new branch and show me
the diff before we commit.
This is the loop we’ll formalize with git in the next module.

title: 2 · Prompting & Directing Agents
section: CLAUDE.md: standing instructions for your project
text:
CLAUDE.md: standing instructions for your project
Repeating “use tidyverse, keep it readable, the data lives in data/” every session is a waste. Put durable facts and preferences in a CLAUDE.md file at the root of your project. Claude Code reads it automatically at the start of every session — it’s persistent context.
A good research CLAUDE.md covers:
# Project: <name>

## What this repo does
One paragraph: the research question and what the code produces.

## Structure
- `data/raw/`    — never edit; source data
- `data/clean/`  — generated by scripts in R/
- `R/`           — numbered pipeline: 01_clean.R, 02_model.R, 03_figs.R
- `figs/`, `tables/` — outputs

## How to run
`source("R/00_run_all.R")` reproduces everything from raw data.

## Conventions
- Language: R (tidyverse). Readable over clever.
- Style: snake_case; one function per task; comment the *why*.
- Figures: colorblind-safe palette; 300 dpi; labelled axes.

## Guardrails
- Never modify anything in data/raw/.
- Don't install packages without asking.
- Make changes on a branch; I review diffs before merging.






NoteCLAUDE.md vs. a skill (preview)



CLAUDE.md = standing context for this project, read every session. A skill (Module 4) = a reusable procedure for a recurring task, invoked when relevant. You’ll write one of each today.








NoteNot Claude-specific: AGENTS.md



The idea is universal, only the filename differs. The cross-tool convention is AGENTS.md — read by OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, and many others (and by Claude Code too). Everything on this page about what to put in the file applies verbatim; if you switch tools, your standing instructions come with you. Writing the file well is the M2 skill — engineering what the model sees — and that transfers everywhere.


You keep a global CLAUDE.md too (mine lives at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) with facts true across all your work — who you are, your stack, your figure preferences. Project files add the specifics.

title: 2 · Prompting & Directing Agents
text:
Reviewing output like a reviewer
Treat the agent’s output like a manuscript you’re reviewing:

Does it answer the question I asked? (Not a nearby one.)
Is the diff minimal and legible? Big surprise diffs are a red flag.
Did it verify? Tests run? Output sane? Row counts right?
Would I be comfortable explaining this in a methods section? If not, ask why it did it that way.







WarningHallucinated specifics



Agents can invent a function argument, a package, a parameter value, or a citation that looks right. Any factual claim — a coefficient, a dose, a reference — gets verified against the source, not accepted because it’s fluent.



What to remember

A prompt = goal + context + constraints + done-condition.
Plan before acting, work in small steps, and make the agent show its work.
One session, one task — start fresh when you switch.
Put durable project facts in CLAUDE.md so you stop repeating yourself.
Review output like a critical reviewer; verify every factual specific.

title: Foundations of Agentic Coding
text:
The shift
For decades: you type every line.
Agentic coding: you describe what you want; the agent writes, runs, and fixes it; you review and decide what to keep.

Your role: author → director.


Value shifts from syntax recall to clear intent, critical review, and control.

title: Foundations of Agentic Coding
text:
Mechanisms, not tools
We teach with Claude Code — but it’s just the current instance.
Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, next year’s tool: same machinery underneath.

Tools and config syntax age fast. Mechanisms don’t.





#
Mechanism




M1
The agent loop


M2
Context is the scarce resource


M3
You are the principal


M4
Verification asymmetry






Framing adapted from Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham, NBER SI 2026 (github.com/paulgp/nber_hf_2026)

title: Foundations of Agentic Coding
text:
M1 · The agent loop
Three things, no magic:

An LLM — turns descriptions into code
Tools — read/write files, run code, search
A loop — act → observe → decide → repeat


   you ─► LLM ─► pick a tool ─► run it ─► read result
           ▲                                 │
           └──────── decide next ◄───────────┘


A chatbot answers. An agent acts, checks its work, and iterates — in your real project.

title: Foundations of Agentic Coding
text:
M2 · Context is scarce
The model reasons only over its context window — what it currently sees.

Too little → it guesses, invents column names
Too much / stale → it loses the thread


The durable skill: staging context — the right files, the data dictionary, the error message, standing instructions written down once.


This skill transfers to every tool. Config syntax doesn’t.

title: Foundations of Agentic Coding
text:
M3 · You are the principal
Delegation economics — same as managing an RA:

Specify the task and the done-condition
Decompose into small, checkable steps
Monitor the diffs, not the vibes
Verify before you accept


Appreciating skills: taste · specification · skepticism
Depreciating skill: typing speed

title: Foundations of Agentic Coding
text:
M4 · Verification asymmetry

Agents excel exactly where checking their work is cheap.


Code runs or it doesn’t. Tests pass or fail. Row counts match or they don’t.
That’s why coding is the breakout agent application.

title: Foundations of Agentic Coding
section: M4 predicts where agents help you
text:
M4 predicts where agents help you



Cheap to verify ✓
Expensive to verify ⚠




Boilerplate & data glue
Causal / statistical judgment


Debugging
Domain facts, parameters, citations


Refactoring
Anything irreversible


Figures & tables
Confidential data (IRB!)


Simulation scaffolding





The estimand is yours — checking it requires exactly the expertise you hoped to save.

title: Foundations of Agentic Coding
text:
The one rule

Never merge what you haven’t reviewed.


Fast + confident + sometimes wrong → keep a review step. That’s why the next big module is git.

title: Foundations of Agentic Coding
text:
The catch: pain points move
Execution got dramatically cheaper. Research didn’t get easier — the pain moved:

Verification debt — production cost collapsed; verification cost didn’t
Judgment still king — design, estimand, model structure; agents default to the well-trodden
Ideas at a premium — cheap execution raises the bar
Data access doesn’t budge — no agent gets you a DUA


Winners redeploy saved time into verification, design, and ideas.

M1: agent = LLM + tools + a loop
M2: context is the scarce resource — stage it
M3: you’re the principal — specify, decompose, monitor, verify
M4: agents excel where verification is cheap
Execution got cheap; verification, judgment, ideas didn’t — spend the savings there
